title: Realtime multiplayer, automation, and you! — Idan Gazit, GitHub

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 46%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: GitHub Next builds developer platform tools—Copilot, Agentic Workflows, ACE—all targeted at software developers as the primary user base. The entire talk is about improving the developer tooling landscape.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The Astro upgrade workflow is a coding assistant that modifies code, fixes breaking changes, verifies builds, and creates PRs. Home Assistant's issue triager is also a coding-adjacent assistant.

summary: Idan Gazit, head of GitHub Next (the team that created Copilot), presents two research prototypes at the AI Engineer conference, framing AI's value through two durable lenses: automation and collaboration. For automation, he demonstrates Agentic Workflows—a system that turns plain-English instructions into Markdown playbooks that compile to GitHub Actions YAML. The headline demo upgrades his Astro website from v5 to v7, finding breaking changes, fixing code, verifying builds, and flagging manual steps. The critical design lesson is that prompt-based guardrails are insufficient because prompt injection can override them; real guardrails are deterministic declarations in YAML front matter covering permissions, allowed tools, network egress, and safe outputs that cap writes to a single pull request. Four security principles are articulated: defense in depth, never trust agents with secrets (secrets stay outside the agent's jail, accessed via a warden pattern), stage and vet all writes, and log everything. The workflow is explicitly allowed to do nothing to prevent denial-of-service against its owner. Agentic Workflows is in public preview, with real-world adoption by the Home Assistant project for automated issue triage. For collaboration, Gazit presents ACE—a Slack-like multiplayer development surface running each session in a cloud microVM. ACE surfaces facts not in code: political constraints, infrastructure decisions, shared plans. Teammates collaboratively edit Markdown plan documents and tell the agent to make the document true. He describes an inversion where improving agents need humans less yet can invoke humans as hands. He closes noting a longitudinal study of ~100 developers found typing is only ~5% of developer work—the only 5% AI tools have addressed so far.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent argument about the next phase of AI in software engineering. The automation concepts (Agentic Workflows, deterministic guardrails, warden pattern, safe outputs, no-op permission) establish that safe autonomous agents require deterministic, compiled security constraints—not prompt-based instructions—because prompt injection fundamentally undermines trust in LLM-interpreted rules. The collaboration concepts (ACE, shared plan documents, ambient awareness, group productivity thesis) extend this to the social dimension: the 5% typing study proves that individual code completion is a small fraction of real developer work, and the remaining 95% is inherently social—planning, review, coordination, and political negotiation. ACE addresses this by making collaboration the substrate for agent direction: shared Markdown documents become executable specs, and ambient awareness reduces misalignment. The human-as-tool inversion ties both lenses together: as agents handle more automation, they need humans less for execution but more for judgment, creating a feedback loop where guardrails ensure agents operate safely autonomously while collaboration surfaces ensure humans remain engaged where their judgment adds the most value. Together, these concepts argue that the industry must move from individual code-completion tools to team-level agent infrastructure with security-by-compilation and collaboration-by-design.
temporalContext: The talk was published August 8, 2026, by the AI Engineer YouTube channel. Agentic Workflows was introduced as a GitHub Next research prototype in August 2025, covered in a February 2026 GitHub Blog article on Continuous AI, and entered public preview in July 2026 per an official GitHub announcement. ACE was first publicly demonstrated by Maggie Appleton at the AI Engineer London Conference on April 9, 2026, and was heading toward technical preview as of August 2026. Research for this annotation was conducted on August 23, 2026.
takeaways: AI's greatest value lies in enabling group productivity, not multiplying individual output
Agentic Workflows turns plain-English instructions into Markdown playbooks; the YAML Actions file is a compiled artifact nobody reads
Prompting an agent to behave is not a guardrail—prompt injection can undo any instruction, letting the fox into the henhouse
Four security principles: defense in depth, never trust agents with secrets, stage and vet all writes, log everything
Secrets stay outside the agent's jail; the agent asks a warden for access, treating any secret an agent can see as already compromised
An automation must be explicitly allowed to do nothing, or it becomes a denial of service against its own owner

concepts.name: Prompt injection vulnerability
concepts.explanation: Prompt-based instructions to an agent can be overridden by injection attacks embedded in tool outputs, user data, or external content the agent processes. This makes prompt-based guardrails unreliable—'letting the fox loose in the henhouse.'
concepts.importance: The fundamental threat model that drives all architectural decisions in the talk: if prompts cannot be trusted, security must be enforced through deterministic, compiled constraints outside the LLM's control.

concepts.name: Agent harness architecture
concepts.explanation: The control-plane design that structures how AI agents execute: declaring permissions, scoping tool access, constraining network egress, limiting outputs, and isolating execution environments. The harness sits between the LLM and the system it operates on.
concepts.importance: Defines the boundary between agent autonomy and safety controls, determining what an agent can and cannot do regardless of what it is prompted to do.

concepts.name: Agentic CI/CD
concepts.explanation: Using AI agents within continuous integration and deployment pipelines to automate tasks requiring basic judgment—dependency upgrades, issue triage, build diagnosis—that previously required human intervention or rigid heuristic scripts.
concepts.importance: Represents the industrialization of software development automation beyond static CI rules, enabling adaptive maintenance workflows.

concepts.name: Multi-agent collaboration surfaces
concepts.explanation: ACE's model where multiple human teammates and coding agents share a single workspace with chat, shared plan documents, ambient awareness, and per-session cloud environments. The collaboration surface erases the boundary between planning, coding, and review.
concepts.importance: Extends AI from individual productivity tools to group productivity infrastructure, addressing the 95% of developer work that is social and coordinative.

concepts.name: Shared plan documents as AI direction interface (spec-based programming)
concepts.explanation: Collaboratively edited Markdown documents serve as executable specifications: teammates edit the plan together, then tell the agent to 'make the document true.' The document becomes the interface between human intent and agent execution.
concepts.importance: Introduces a paradigm where natural-language specifications written by humans become the directive that autonomous agents execute against, bridging planning and implementation.

concepts.name: Human-as-tool inversion
concepts.explanation: As agents improve at understanding goals, they need humans less for execution, yet can invoke humans as 'hands' when they encounter tasks requiring human judgment, physical action, or authorization—reversing the traditional human-directs-agent relationship.
concepts.importance: Reframes the long-term human-agent relationship: rather than humans delegating to AI, AI agents orchestrate human involvement on-demand.

concepts.name: Multi-engine agent design
concepts.explanation: Agentic Workflows supports multiple LLM backends (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) rather than being tied to a single model, allowing workflow portability across engine providers.
concepts.importance: Architectural decision enabling engine-agnostic agent workflows, preventing lock-in and allowing optimal model selection per task.

concepts.name: Longitudinal developer productivity study (5% typing)
concepts.explanation: A longitudinal study of approximately 100 developers over thousands of hours found that hands-on-keyboard typing represents only about 5% of developer work. AI tools have so far only addressed that 5%, leaving the remaining 95%—planning, review, coordination, debugging—untouched.
concepts.importance: Quantifies the gap between what current AI tools address and the full scope of developer work, motivating the shift toward collaboration and automation beyond code completion.

concepts.name: Group productivity as primary AI value
concepts.explanation: The thesis that AI's greatest value is not multiplying individual output but enabling groups of people to do more together through shared context, aligned plans, and coordinated action.
concepts.importance: Reframes the target of AI development tools from individual augmentation to team-level productivity, guiding the design of ACE and future collaboration surfaces.

concepts.name: Ambient team awareness in agent workspaces
concepts.explanation: ACE surfaces what teammates are working on in real time, providing contextual awareness without explicit communication—the system shows who is editing what, running which agents, and addressing which issues.
concepts.importance: Enables coordination in multi-agent, multi-human environments by making work visible, reducing misalignment and duplicated effort.

concepts.name: Agentic Workflows pipeline (Markdown-to-YAML compilation)
concepts.explanation: A system where plain-English instructions are expanded into Markdown playbooks that compile into GitHub Actions YAML. The Markdown is the human-editable source; the YAML is a compiled artifact nobody reads. The pipeline includes deterministic guardrails in front matter: permissions, allowed tools, reachable network destinations, and safe-output limits.
concepts.importance: Introduces a new compilation paradigm for CI/CD where natural language is the source of truth and the execution manifest is generated, bringing testable, reviewable automation to agent-driven workflows.

concepts.name: Deterministic guardrails via YAML front matter
concepts.explanation: Instead of prompting an agent to behave (which prompt injection can override), guardrails are declared as deterministic metadata in YAML front matter: permissions, allowed tools, network egress allow-lists, and safe outputs. These are compiled into the execution environment, not interpreted by the LLM.
concepts.importance: The core architectural insight of the talk: security constraints on agents must be machine-enforced, not prompt-based, because prompt injection makes LLM-interpreted instructions unreliable.

concepts.name: Markdown-as-source, YAML-as-compiled-artifact
concepts.explanation: Markdown documentation serves as the editable source code; the generated GitHub Actions YAML is a compiled artifact that humans never need to inspect, analogous to how developers write source code rather than machine code.
concepts.importance: Inverts the traditional relationship between configuration and documentation, making the human-readable format the primary artifact and the machine-readable format derived.

concepts.name: Secret warden pattern
concepts.explanation: Secrets are kept outside the agent's execution boundary (jail). When an agent needs to use a secret to call an external service, it must ask a warden service that validates, scopes, and logs the request. Any secret an agent can directly see is treated as already compromised.
concepts.importance: A practical architecture pattern for managing secrets in autonomous agent systems, preventing agents from exfiltrating or misusing credentials even when compromised via prompt injection.

concepts.name: Safe outputs constraint (single-PR write limit)
concepts.explanation: The agent's write-back is capped to at most one new pull request. The coding agent itself does not have direct write permission; all changes must go through the PR review pipeline. This limits the blast radius of any single agent execution.
concepts.importance: Constrains the damage autonomy can cause in CI/CD pipelines by channeling all mutations through human-reviewable artifacts.

concepts.name: Defense in depth for agent systems
concepts.explanation: Layered security combining multiple independent controls: least-privilege tokens, allow-listed tools, network egress restrictions, secret isolation via warden, staged writes, and comprehensive logging. No single layer is trusted to be sufficient.
concepts.importance: Provides redundancy so that compromise of one control does not lead to total system failure—a critical principle for autonomous systems operating on production code.

concepts.name: Explicit no-op permission
concepts.explanation: An automation must be explicitly allowed to do nothing. Without this, agents generate noise and unnecessary work, effectively creating a denial-of-service against the workflow owner who must review every output.
concepts.importance: A subtle but essential design principle: the absence of action is a valid and often correct outcome that must be a first-class option in automation systems.

concepts.name: Staged writes with human-visible artifacts
concepts.explanation: All agent mutations produce human-readable artifacts—pull requests, comments, and logs—rather than silent changes. The agent never directly mutates state; it proposes changes that are staged for human review.
concepts.importance: Ensures auditability and maintains human-in-the-loop review for autonomous changes to production systems.

concepts.name: Network egress allow-listing for agents
concepts.explanation: Guardrails declaratively specify which network destinations an agent may reach, preventing data exfiltration to unauthorized endpoints even if the agent is compromised via prompt injection.
concepts.importance: Controls the network attack surface of LLM-based agents that may attempt to send data to external servers.

concepts.name: Cloud microVM isolation for development sessions
concepts.explanation: In ACE, each development session runs in its own cloud microVM on an isolated git branch, providing strong sandboxing between concurrent teammates and agents. This enables safe multi-tenant agent execution.
concepts.importance: Provides the isolation guarantees necessary for multiple agents and humans to operate concurrently in a shared development surface without interfering.

concepts.name: GitHub Actions as agent execution runtime
concepts.explanation: Existing CI/CD infrastructure (GitHub Actions) serves as the execution environment for agentic workflows, leveraging trusted, observable, and already-deployed infrastructure rather than building new agent runtime systems.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how to deploy autonomous agents using existing, proven infrastructure, reducing operational risk and adoption barriers.

concepts.name: Issue triage automation (Home Assistant pattern)
concepts.explanation: A production agentic workflow deployed by the Home Assistant project that reads Python stack traces in GitHub issues, classifies whether bugs are first-party or third-party, and auto-closes third-party issues—demonstrating real-world autonomous issue management at scale.
concepts.importance: Validates agentic workflows as practical production tools beyond demos, showing measurable automation of software maintenance tasks.

sections.title: Introduction and Durable Themes
sections.summary: Idan Gazit introduces himself as leader of GitHub Next, GitHub's exploratory research team. He explains their mission of scouting future developer tools and identifies durable themes: AI moved from personal productivity toward group productivity, and the greatest value comes from enabling groups rather than multiplying individuals.

sections.title: Two Lenses: Automation and Collaboration
sections.summary: Frames two lenses for future work. Automation: the software industry is still pre-industrial since prior automations were mere heuristics; now AI can automate tasks requiring basic judgment. Collaboration: faster processes mean small misalignments snowball into wasted work. He previews two prototypes: Agentic Workflows and ACE.

sections.title: Agentic Workflows Prototype and Demo Setup
sections.summary: Demonstrates an Agentic Workflow for upgrading his Astro-based personal website. He wrote roughly three lines of plain English—like a Slack message to a junior developer—and Copilot expanded it into a full Markdown playbook. The Markdown is the source; the YAML Actions file is a compiled artifact nobody reads.

sections.title: Guardrails Design
sections.summary: Explains that prompting an agent to behave is not a guardrail because prompt injection can override it. Real guardrails are deterministic declarations in YAML front matter: permissions, allowed tools, reachable network destinations, and safe outputs limiting the agent to a single pull request. The agent is explicitly allowed to do nothing to prevent denial-of-service noise.

sections.title: Demo Results and Workflow Library
sections.summary: Shows the workflow handling a minor release and a major upgrade from Astro 5 to 7. Presents a library of reusable workflows: issue triager, repo assist swarms, CI doctor, daily status reports, and PM tasks.

sections.title: Security Principles and Home Assistant Example
sections.summary: Articulates four security principles: defense in depth, never trust agents with secrets (treat visible secrets as compromised), stage and vet all writes, and log everything. Secrets stay outside the agent's jail, accessed via a warden. Home Assistant built a workflow that reads Python stack traces in issues to determine first-party vs third-party bugs and auto-closes third-party issues. Agentic Workflows is in public preview.

sections.title: Collaboration and ACE Introduction
sections.summary: Frames collaboration: software building was once solitary but now planning, review, and iteration are continuous with AI. ACE resembles Slack but surfaces facts not in code—political considerations, infrastructure deals, team dynamics—because agents already read code.

sections.title: ACE Demo: Multiplayer Development
sections.summary: Demos ACE running in cloud microVMs. Teammates chat, run dev servers, and edit shared Markdown plan documents together. The agent reads the entire conversation backscroll and the edited plan to act. Shows ambient awareness of teammates' work and envisions automations surfacing in the interface.

sections.title: Inversion of the Human-Agent Relationship and Closing
sections.summary: Describes an inversion: as agents improve at understanding goals, they need humans less, yet can invoke humans as needed. Closes with a longitudinal study of ~100 developers over thousands of hours finding typing is 5% of the work; AI has only addressed that 5%. Invites attendees to try both prototypes.

organization.name: GitHub Next
organization.summary: GitHub Next is a research lab within GitHub, described on its official homepage as 'a team of researchers and engineers at GitHub, exploring things beyond the adjacent possible.' It prototypes future developer tools and technologies, with successful incubations including Copilot, Copilot Workspace, GitHub Spark, and Agentic Workflows. The GitHub Next people page lists 15 team members including Idan Gazit (Head of GitHub Next since December 2024), Maggie Appleton, Don Syme, and Russell Horton. GitHub Next created both prototypes demonstrated in the video: Agentic Workflows (in public preview as of July 2026) and ACE (Agent Collaboration Environment, earlier-stage research not listed on the projects page).

technologies.label: Agentic Workflows
technologies.summary: Agentic Workflows is a GitHub Next research prototype that turns plain-English instructions into Markdown playbooks that compile into GitHub Actions YAML. The Markdown is the human-editable source; the YAML is a compiled artifact nobody reads. Guardrails are declared deterministically in YAML front matter covering permissions, allowed tools, reachable network destinations, and safe outputs capping write-back to a single pull request. The system is multi-engine (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex). The headline demo upgrades an Astro website from v5 to v7, finding breaking changes, fixing code, verifying builds, and flagging manual steps. Real-world adoption includes Home Assistant's automated issue triage. It entered public preview in July 2026 per an official GitHub announcement.
technologies.role: Primary technology for the automation lens; headline demo upgrades Astro from v5 to v7, with a library of reusable workflows including issue triager, CI doctor, and daily status reports

technologies.label: ACE (Agent Collaboration Environment)
technologies.summary: ACE is a GitHub Next research prototype for real-time multiplayer development with coding agents. It resembles a chat app but runs every session in a cloud microVM on an isolated git branch. ACE surfaces facts not in code—political constraints, infrastructure decisions, shared plans—because agents can already read code. Teammates collaboratively edit Markdown plan documents and tell the agent to make the document true. It provides ambient awareness of teammates' work. ACE was first publicly demoed by Maggie Appleton at the AI Engineer London Conference in April 2026. As of August 2026, it is heading toward technical preview but is not yet listed on the GitHub Next Projects page, indicating earlier-stage research than Agentic Workflows.
technologies.role: Second prototype for the collaboration lens; live demo of multiplayer session editing shared Markdown plan documents and directing the agent to execute the edited plan; demonstrates ambient team awareness

technologies.label: Deterministic Agent Guardrails Architecture
technologies.primary: Deterministic guardrails via YAML front matter
technologies.summary: The talk's central architectural insight: prompt-based guardrails are unreliable because prompt injection can override any LLM-interpreted instruction. Instead, deterministic guardrails are declared as compiled metadata in YAML front matter—permissions, allowed tools, network egress allow-lists, and safe outputs capping writes to a single pull request. Four security principles are articulated: (1) defense in depth, (2) never trust agents with secrets—secrets stay outside the agent's jail and are accessed via a warden, (3) stage and vet all writes as human-visible artifacts, (4) log everything. The system is explicitly allowed to do nothing to prevent denial-of-service noise. This architecture is embedded in Agentic Workflows but represents a general design pattern for any autonomous agent system.
technologies.role: Explains why prompting agents to behave fails (prompt injection) and demonstrates deterministic YAML front-matter guardrails as the secure alternative; articulates four security principles with the warden pattern for secrets and explicit no-op permission

technologies.label: GitHub Actions as Agent Execution Runtime
technologies.summary: GitHub Actions is the CI/CD platform that serves as the execution runtime for Agentic Workflows. The talk describes a paradigm shift: Markdown is the source code, and the GitHub Actions YAML file is a compiled artifact nobody reads—similar to how developers write source code rather than machine code. By compiling to Actions YAML, agent automations inherit all the observability, reliability, and operational maturity of GitHub's existing CI/CD pipeline. This demonstrates how to deploy autonomous agents using existing, proven infrastructure rather than building new agent runtime systems.
technologies.role: The compilation target and execution runtime for Agentic Workflows; the YAML Actions file is described as a compiled artifact nobody reads, establishing the Markdown-as-source paradigm

challengeSeeds: Design YAML front-matter guardrails for an agentic workflow that triages GitHub issues by reading Python stack traces—declare permissions, allowed tools, network egress destinations, and output limits. Justify each choice and explain what happens when the workflow encounters an ambiguous trace.

Contrast a prompt-based instruction ('do not exfiltrate secrets') against a deterministic front-matter constraint (network egress allow-list with no public internet access). Which prompt-injection attack vectors does each approach fail against, and why?

Implement a reference warden service in your preferred language that accepts secret-access requests from agents, validates the request against a declared policy, logs the access, and returns time-scoped credentials. What audit fields should the log contain, and how would you detect anomalous access patterns?

Given a real GitHub repository, author a Markdown playbook that upgrades a dependency and verifies builds. Run it via the gh aw CLI and inspect the compiled YAML. Identify three guardrails that would need to change if the workflow also needed to publish a package to a registry.

Propose a new ACE session feature that addresses one of the remaining 95% of developer work (planning, review, team coordination, or debugging). Specify the user interaction model, the agent's role, and the safety guardrails that would be required.

Critique the Home Assistant issue-triage workflow: what happens when a stack trace is ambiguous between first-party and third-party code? Design a fallback strategy that keeps the human in the loop without creating automation denial-of-service noise.

Given that an automation must be explicitly allowed to do nothing, design a monitoring and alerting system that distinguishes between 'agent correctly chose to do nothing' and 'agent failed to execute'. What log structure and observability signals support both cases?

entities.name: Idan Gazit
entities.relation: Speaker in the video. Idan Gazit leads GitHub Next, the research team that created Copilot and incubated Agentic Workflows and ACE. His LinkedIn profile confirms he has been Head of GitHub Next since December 2024, having previously served as Senior Director of Research (2022-2024) and Director of Research (2020-2022). Per his LinkedIn bio, he joined GitHub Next at its inception (when it was the Office of the CTO) and helped boot it up; successful incubations include Copilot, Copilot Workspace, and GitHub Spark.

entities.name: GitHub Next
entities.relation: GitHub Next is the research team within GitHub led by Idan Gazit. It created the two prototypes demonstrated in the video (Agentic Workflows and ACE) and previously incubated Copilot. Per Idan's LinkedIn bio: 'GitHub Next is a group of researchers and engineers tasked with exploring strategic technology bets for GitHub. Successful incubations from our group include Copilot, Copilot Workspace, GitHub Spark, and many more.' The githubnext.com projects page confirms Agentic Workflows is officially tracked as an Aug 2025 Research Prototype.

entities.name: Agentic Workflows
entities.relation: First prototype demonstrated in the video. According to the GitHub Next project page, Agentic Workflows is a research prototype (Aug 2025) enabling natural-language programming over GitHub Actions. Markdown serves as the source of truth; YAML Actions files are compiled artifacts. The design grounds deterministic guardrails in front matter (permissions, safe-outputs, tools, network destinations) rather than prompts. The safe-outputs constraint caps write-back to at most one pull request. A July 2026 GitHub official announcement (reposted by Russell Horton, GitHub Staff Security Analyst) confirms Agentic Workflows is in public preview, matching the transcript's status claim. The talk's headline demo upgrades Astro from version 5 to 7 using this prototype.

entities.name: ACE (Agent Collaboration Environment)
entities.relation: Second prototype demonstrated in the video. ACE is a multiplayer development surface with Slack-like chat, shared Markdown plan documents, and per-session cloud microVMs on isolated git branches. Confirmed as a GitHub Next research prototype by the GitHub Next talks page (Maggie Appleton's April 2026 ACE talk) and multiple secondary sources (BuzzRAG, Tokenless, AIssential, Alcreon). ACE = Agent Collaboration Environment is corroborated externally. Per secondary sources, ACE was heading toward technical preview in April 2026; the transcript's claim that ACE 'enters technical preview later' is consistent with this status. Notably, ACE is NOT listed on the GitHub Next Projects page, suggesting it remains in earlier-stage research than Agentic Workflows.

entities.name: Maggie Appleton
entities.relation: Related context. Maggie Appleton (GitHub Next) previously presented ACE at the AI Engineer London Conference on April 9, 2026. The video being annotated (iQ5xldZ9StU) is a separate, later talk by Idan Gazit that also demonstrates ACE. Maggie's earlier talk provides the most detailed public description of ACE's architecture and goals to date, which is used here as contextual corroboration of the transcript's ACE descriptions.

resources.why: Ace is a realtime, multiplayer coding agent workspace built within GitHub Next. Sessions are Slack-like channels where teammates and coding agents collaborate in shared cloud environments.

resources.title: Idan Gazit's InfoQ Profile
resources.why: Idan Gazit is Senior Director of Research at GitHub Next, an early member of the team who leads the Developer Experience research team. He is a hybrid designer/developer interested in data display, typography, and color.

resources.title: Realtime multiplayer, automation, and you! — Idan Gazit, GitHub
resources.why: GitHub Next's Idan Gazit demos Agentic Workflows and Ace. Agentic Workflows compiles plain-English instructions into scheduled guardrailed automations (already in public preview). Ace is a Slack-shaped environment for real-time multiplayer development running in cloud micro-VMs (technical preview expected later in August 2026).

evidence.excerpt: the greatest value doesn't come from multiplying me into more me. It comes from enabling groups of people to do more.
evidence.supports: Core thesis: group productivity over individual productivity

evidence.excerpt: if GitHub Actions and Copilot had a baby together, and it ran on markdown, this is what it is
evidence.supports: Agentic Workflows concept as Markdown-driven Actions

evidence.excerpt: if you're prompting the guardrails at the agent, you're effectively letting the fox loose in the henhouse. It's not actually a guard rail.
evidence.supports: Prompt-based guardrails are ineffective against injection

evidence.excerpt: explicitly said you're allowed to do nothing, right? Which sounds silly, but it actually matters because in a world where I have lots of automations, the last thing I want is noise.
evidence.supports: Allowing no-op prevents automation denial of service against the owner

evidence.excerpt: the markdown is the source code. The YAML is like a compiled artifact. You never look at it.
evidence.supports: Markdown as source, YAML as compiled artifact in Agentic Workflows

evidence.excerpt: Never trust agents with secrets. If an agent can know a secret, that secret, you need to treat it as if it's already been compromised.
evidence.supports: Secrets visible to agents are effectively compromised

evidence.excerpt: the secrets are all kept outside of the agent's jail, and when the agent wants to use the secret to call something, it needs to ask the warden
evidence.supports: Warden pattern for secret access outside agent jail

evidence.excerpt: anything that's in code, any fact that's in code, the agents can figure out by reading the code. What's left are the things that are not in code, like political considerations.
evidence.supports: ACE surfaces non-code facts: politics, infrastructure deals, team dynamics

evidence.excerpt: we've updated the plan, do it.
evidence.supports: Shared document editing as the interface for directing AI

evidence.excerpt: hands-on keyboard typing part is 5% of the time. Now, AI has to help me with the other 95%.
evidence.supports: Typing is 5% of developer work; AI must address the remaining 95%
